source_readings.reading: Primary preface, title page and chapter I opening read in the Gutenberg transcription. Statutory and documentary research is his stated method; the preface warns of missing economic data. Remaining chapters, numerical findings and period racial assumptions are not independently verified.

Forethought (dated 1 February 1903) and chapter I read in Gutenberg transcription. Double consciousness and the combined claims of work, culture, liberty and education are his formulations. Book publication year checked against existing LOC record dubois_souls. This is not a complete reading of all fourteen chapters.

Publisher-authorized introduction excerpt read in full. Anderson interprets Du Bois’s 1899 social survey through racial exclusion in employment and its contemporary relevance. The 1899 date is explicitly confirmed; this reading is Anderson’s, not a new full reading of Du Bois’s book or Eaton’s separately credited domestic-service investigation.

Open-access abstract, introduction and opening World War I section read on Cambridge Core. Williams characterizes the 1935 reinterpretation of Reconstruction as multiracial democracy defeated and relates its writing to Du Bois’s wartime political development. Black Reconstruction itself remains unread in this pass. Online 2022 and print-issue 2023 dates are distinguished.

Preface (dated 31 March 1918), contents and opening of chapter I read. Woodson connects the wartime migration with earlier movements and explicitly offers an accessible, provisional synthesis. Original 1918 publication checked against LOC https://www.loc.gov/item/18017856/. No independent verification of the whole book’s demographic claims or maps.

Public-domain transcription: Woodson’s own preface and chapter I read; the separately headed later introduction is not treated as his writing. The 1933 date checked against the National Park Service bibliography. His criticism of educational dependence and exclusion of Black history is stated as his argument; historical racial terminology belongs to the original text.

Institutional page read for scholarly publishing dates (Journal of Negro History 1916; Associated Publishers 1921; Negro History Bulletin 1937), its bibliography and Woodson’s 1926 public-education statement. Quoted historical statements remain mediated by the NPS; no claim of sole invention of Black history is accepted.

Article text read at pp. 912–916 and 919–920 in the public institutional copy at https://blackwomenintheblackfreedomstruggle.voices.wooster.edu/wp-content/uploads/sites/210/2019/01/Darlene-Clark-Hine_Rape-and-the-Inner-Lives-of-Black-Women.pdf. Publisher metadata confirms July 1989, pp.912–920; publisher body unavailable. The 1988 conference version is explicitly earlier. Her migration explanation supplements rather than replaces economic motives; she acknowledges limits of the dissemblance concept.

Institutional-repository abstract read in full; PDF download returned 403 and was not read. Wintz places the 1989 book in revisionist nursing history and describes its emphasis on racial/gender barriers and Black nurses’ agency. Claims are attributed to Wintz’s published abstract; no full-book reading or independent professional-history reconstruction is claimed.

Oxford Academic’s indexed “Extract,” headed “Preface: The Meta-Argument,” read: Hine makes parallel Black professional organizations a condition of effective challenges to white supremacy. The full article was blocked and remains unread. Publication is dated March 2003; a separately delivered OAH address is not silently dated as publication.

Read pp.7–14, especially pp.9 and 11–14, in the public McGill English Department copy https://www.mcgill.ca/english/files/english/hartman_venus_in_two_acts.pdf. The method includes restraint and acknowledged failure; it does not authorize invented voices as recovered fact. Earlier source p4a_hartman_venus_2008 remains the record of the previous metadata-only check; this new witness records the later passage reading. The MoMA authorized reprint could not be fetched; it is not claimed as read.

Interview read in full. Hartman distinguishes nonfiction from novelistic form, state case files from slavery’s scarcer archive, and ordinary Black women’s experiments from elite-centered histories. Her explicit criticism of Du Bois’s class/gender judgments is read in the answer beginning “Du Bois is so important”; it is dated to this 2020 statement, not asserted as a passage independently read in Wayward Lives.

Opening discussion of archival grief, Lose Your Mother and Wayward Lives, and answers on the term “wayward” read. Her memoir’s closing relational argument is known through her retrospective account, not a new full reading of the 2007 book. Original works dated 1997, 2007 and 2019 in the introduction, consistent with MacArthur’s existing bibliography.

Author abstract and publication metadata read in Rutgers’s research portal. Fuentes contests triumphalist interpretations of Polgreen by tracing archival representation and her exploitation of other women. Article body unread; argument is limited to the abstract’s stated intervention. DOI 10.1111/j.1468-0424.2010.01616.x.

Publisher-authorized excerpt read in full. Fuentes describes the lack of enslaved women’s own accounts, changing the archival gaze, limits of recovery and risks of narrating violence. This is selected book text, not the whole book; excerpt web date 2017 is separate from original book publication in 2016.

Interview read in full. Fuentes explains her focus on Bridgetown, critiques the rural/urban leniency dichotomy and empirical demands that erase fragmentary lives, and describes unnamed scholarly pushback. Those objections are her report, not independently read replies; no invented opponent or critique arrow is added.

Publisher description, complete contents, editor/contributor credits and publication metadata read. Date 20 December 2016. Joint editorship, committee research, and named chapter authors are distinct; White wrote the introduction, and Fuentes is not credited as sole author of the findings. Book chapters unread; public-history contribution is scoped to the documented collaborative publication and its stated public institutional purpose.

Author’s roundtable contribution read in full. She reads Sowande’ Mustakeem’s Slavery at Sea, questions abstraction and reenactment of archival violence, and explicitly identifies Hartman’s “Venus in Two Acts” as inspiration for the jointly edited slavery/archive issue. Mustakeem’s book and the entire issue remain unread in this pass.

Author bibliography explicitly lists the 2016 History of the Present “Slavery and the Archive” special issue as coedited with Brian Connolly. USF’s institutional record https://digitalcommons.usf.edu/hty_facpub/171/ confirms both introduction authors, Fall 2016, vol.6 no.2, pp.105–116 and DOI 10.5406/historypresent.6.2.0105. These records establish date/credits only; the full introduction and issue remain unread.

Hine nursing book is mediated by Wintz’s abstract; 2003 address only its opening extract. Hine Sight original/reissue dates remain unresolved and are not put on chronology.
